name: Two-Way Switch
tagline: Three terminals instead of two: two of these and a pair of strappers let you work one light from two places.
terminals: COM — common, from the supply or to the lamp
L1 — strapper to the other switch
Earth — plate earth where a metal plate is used
parts: Faceplate — one or two gang, two-way on every gang
Rockers — one or two, each switching between L1 and L2
Four fixing screws on a two-gang plate
Three terminals per gang: COM, L1, L2
Strappers — the two conductors running between the switches
safety: COM is not interchangeable with L1 and L2. Landing the supply on a strapper terminal produces a switch that works from one end only, or one that blows the fuse when both switches are operated. Identify COM (it is usually a different coloured terminal) before you connect anything.

points.label: Faceplate
points.detail: A two-gang plate carries two independent switches on one back box — one for the landing light, one for the hall, for example. Each gang switches its own circuit; they do not work together unless you wire them as two-way.

points.label: Left rocker
points.detail: Each rocker throws its common terminal between L1 and L2. Which of the two strappers is live at any moment depends on the position of both switches, which is exactly why the circuit works either way round.

points.label: Right rocker
points.detail: The second gang. On a staircase the two switches sit at opposite ends of the run and the two strappers run between them; the lamp is connected to whichever switch is more convenient.

points.label: Fixing screws
points.detail: Four screws on a two-gang plate. Long plate screws through a deep back box can foul the conductors behind, so use the screws supplied with the accessory.

points.label: Terminals (COM, L1, L2)
points.detail: Three terminals per gang. COM is the common — the moving contact — and it is the one that carries the supply in at one end and feeds the lamp at the other. L1 and L2 are the strappers and are interchangeable with each other.

points.label: Strapper identification
points.detail: Both strappers are live in one switch position or the other, so both need brown sleeving at each end. You cannot identify a strapper by testing for voltage — only by tracing it.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of a two-way switch showing the rocker, changeover contact, common terminal and the two strapper terminals

cutawayPoints.label: Rocker
cutawayPoints.detail: Drives the same over-centre mechanism as a one-way switch, so the contacts snap across rather than following your finger. The feel is identical; what is behind it is not.

cutawayPoints.label: Changeover contact
cutawayPoints.detail: One moving contact tipping between two fixed ones — a single-pole, double-throw switch. The common is always connected to one of the two strappers, never to both and never to neither, which is what lets either of two switches complete the circuit to the lamp.

cutawayPoints.label: Pivot and spring carrier
cutawayPoints.detail: Holds the moving contact against a fixed contact with real pressure. Two-way switching means the contact spends its life alternating between the two strappers, so a worn pivot shows up as intermittent lighting at one end of the landing long before it fails outright.

cutawayPoints.label: Common terminal
cutawayPoints.detail: Marked COM, and it is the one that matters: it takes either the supply or the switched live to the lamp, while L1 and L2 are interchangeable strappers. Wiring to the wrong terminal is the classic two-way fault — the light works from one switch and not the other.

cutawayPoints.label: L1 and L2 terminals
cutawayPoints.detail: The two strapper terminals, carrying the pair of conductors that run between the two switches. They are electrically identical, so it does not matter which is which at either end — what matters is that both strappers go strapper to strapper and the commons are at the supply and the load.

cutawayPoints.label: Fixing screws
cutawayPoints.detail: Two screws into the back box lugs, and the reason a deeper box is often needed: a two-way plate carries three conductors per gang instead of two, and cramming them behind a shallow box is what cracks faceplates and works terminals loose.
